You can really fuck up rotating tires. But make sure you:

Scrape off brush off loose rust or debris from the face on the axle where the wheel smashes up against as you tighten the lug nuts (not as critical if you don't live in the rust belt)

Make sure if you're tires have directiinal tread that you don't install the wheel backwards. Basically don't install the left side tires to the right side and vice versa. Otherwise, rotate them per the owners manual. I think typically it's: bring the front tires straight back and bring the back tires diagonally to the front.

Other tip, break the lugs loose before you jack it up. They won't try to spin as easy then to oppose you trying to turn a nut.

When you tighten the lug nuts, first snug them in a criss cross pattern. Can't always do this perfecr on a five lug car but that's okay. Then once all of the lugs on all wheels are SNUGGED, lower the car and TORQUE them all to the service manual, if given a range for torque, I aim for a value in the middle (if you don't have a Hanes manual go buy one for $20). Torque them in a criss cross pattern. As you tighten some, it relieves pressure against other lugs straight across which is why I say tighten in a criss cross pattern. Lot of people just tighten them as hard as they can instead of torquing, I'm an engineer though and I know they chose that torque range for a reason. Then you don't have to wonder later if they're tight enough either.

Last but not least, I'd personally suggest you use "anti seize" on the threads of the lug studs. It's a silvery metallic paste that prevents rust from binding the lug on and potentially creating a huge headache. You don't need a lot of it and it usually is good for a 3 years or more before reapication is necessary. Also don't get it on your hands because it will end up on everything you touch including clothes and it doesn't come out of clothes too well. Some debate whether it's okay to use this on the studs bc it lubricates the threads and you could potentially overtighten but have the torque wrench read the same value, but I figure the difference is miniscule and me or my dad have had issues with it for the 20 years I've been doing it or the 40 years he's been doing it.

 

Next up: brake work. It's super easy but it's something you might want to have some that k ows what they're doing, monitor your work the first few times. It's really quite easy (disc brakes: rotors and pads) and saves you about $400. You just need to make sure you torque stuff correctly when done. A Hanes manual will walk you through it step by step. One thing I'd suggest is again, any surface that is getting pinched or pressure against it, scrape and brush debris and surface rust from it. Otherwise if you tighten parts with rust between them, vibration over time allows that rust and debris to work out, and now there's a gap and the part is now loose.
